stops.title: The Little Ice Age
stops.blurb: Between the 1400s and the 1700s, the climate in many regions turned colder, with several especially chilly spells. Many historians link the cold to failed harvests, famines, revolts, wars and epidemics, and point to a wave of crises in the mid-1600s. But the cold did not strike everywhere at once: the coldest decades came in the 1400s in the Pacific and the 1600s in north-western Europe.
stops.debate: How far the cold caused the crises is argued. Some researchers stress that political and economic choices made societies vulnerable or resilient, and Koch and colleagues link part of the cooling to forests regrowing in the depopulated Americas.

stops.title: Ottomans, Safavids and Mughals
stops.blurb: In 1453 the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II captured Constantinople and made it his capital; over time it came to be called Istanbul. In 1501 Ismail was crowned the first Safavid shah of Iran, and his successor Abbas moved the capital to Isfahan in 1597–98. In India, Babur defeated the Lodi sultan by 1527, and his grandson Akbar built the Mughal Empire.

stops.title: By sea around Africa to India

place.name: Cape of Good Hope, South Africa

stops.blurb: Portuguese crews had been sailing south along the West African coast since the mid-1400s. In 1488 Bartolomeu Dias rounded the Cape of Good Hope, the southern end of the continent. In 1497 Vasco da Gama followed, called at Mombasa and Malindi, where he hired an experienced navigator, and in May 1498 reached Calicut in India, a great port of the spice trade.

stops.title: Across the Atlantic and around the world
stops.blurb: In 1492 Christopher Columbus, sailing for the Spanish crown, reached Guanahani in the Bahamas, home of the Taíno, the most numerous people of the Caribbean. He believed to the end that he had reached Asia. In 1519 five ships and 237 men left Seville under Ferdinand Magellan. One ship and 18 men came back in 1522, the first crew to sail around the world.
stops.dateNote: Magellan himself was killed in 1521 at Mactan in the Philippines, fighting forces led by Lapulapu; Juan Sebastián de Elcano brought the last ship home.

stops.title: The Columbian Exchange
stops.blurb: After 1492, crops, germs, ideas and people crossed the oceans between the Americas and the rest of the world. Maize, potatoes, sweet potatoes and cassava became staple foods in Africa, Asia and Europe, and chili peppers changed cooking from Hungary to Thailand. Wheat, sugar cane, coffee and bananas went the other way. So did smallpox, measles and other diseases new to the Americas.
stops.debate: How much the new crops raised Old World populations is still being measured. Nunn and Qian estimate the potato alone explains about an eighth of the population increase where it could be grown.

stops.title: The Great Dying in the Americas
stops.blurb: Smallpox, measles, typhus and other diseases from Afro-Eurasia reached peoples in the Americas who had never met them. Epidemics came in waves, alongside conquest and war. A 2019 review estimates that about 90 percent of the Indigenous population died within a century of 1492, some 56 million people. Central Mexico, home to just under 15 million people in 1519, had about 1.5 million a century later.
stops.debate: Published estimates of the population in 1492 range from about 8 million to over 110 million. Koch and colleagues combine them into a middle estimate of about 60 million.

links.label: Population history of the Indigenous peoples of the Americas

stops.title: The transatlantic slave trade
stops.blurb: Between the early 1500s and 1866, ships from Europe and the Americas carried about 12.5 million enslaved Africans across the Atlantic; about 10.7 million survived the voyage. Some 4.7 million were taken before 1750, and the trade grew larger after that. West-Central Africa was the largest source. About 95 percent of the captives were landed in the Caribbean and South America, most of them in sugar-growing regions.
stops.dateNote: Figures are the SlaveVoyages estimates of captives embarked and landed, built from records of about 36,000 voyages.

stops.title: Printing and the Reformation
stops.blurb: Printing with movable metal type spread across Europe from Mainz in the late 1400s. Between 1500 and 1600, cities that had a press in the 1400s grew about 60 percent faster than similar cities without one. On 31 October 1517 Martin Luther published 95 theses challenging the sale of indulgences, generally seen as the start of the Protestant Reformation. Towns with early presses were more likely to turn Protestant.
stops.debate: How much printing caused the Reformation is argued. Rubin estimates that cities with a press by 1500 were at least 29 percentage points more likely to be Protestant by 1600.

stops.title: The fall of the Aztec and Inca empires
stops.blurb: In 1519 Hernán Cortés landed in Mexico. He gained many Indigenous allies, above all Tlaxcala, a long-time enemy of the Mexica. Smallpox weakened Tenochtitlan's defenders, and the city fell after a siege in 1521. Between 1532 and 1533 Francisco Pizarro's small force, arriving during an Inca civil war, captured and executed the ruler Atahualpa despite a huge ransom, then took Cusco.
stops.debate: Why so few Spaniards won is still argued: accounts variously stress steel and horses, Indigenous allies, disease, and divisions within the two empires.

links.label: Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire

stops.title: A new science: from Copernicus to Newton
stops.blurb: In 1543 Nicolaus Copernicus published a book placing the Sun, not the Earth, near the centre of the universe. In 1610 Galileo described mountains on the Moon and four moons circling Jupiter, seen through his telescope; in 1633 the Inquisition condemned him. The Royal Society first met in London in 1660. Newton's Principia of 1687 showed one law of gravity governing planets, comets and tides.

stops.title: Silver, Potosí and the first global economy
stops.blurb: In 1545 rich silver ore was found in the Cerro Rico, a mountain at Potosí in the Andes. From 1573 a forced labour draft, the mita, sent Indigenous men to its mines, and by 1592 the city held nearly 100,000 people. China had moved its money and taxes onto silver, which made silver worth more there. American and Japanese silver flowed towards China by every route.

stops.title: Tokugawa Japan and Qing China
stops.blurb: In 1600 Tokugawa Ieyasu won a decisive battle at Sekigahara, and in 1603 he became shogun, Japan's military ruler; his descendants governed for over 250 years. By the late 1630s foreigners were barred, except Chinese and Dutch merchants trading at Nagasaki. In 1644 the Manchus, from north-east of the Great Wall, conquered the Ming and founded the Qing dynasty, which lasted nearly 300 years.

stops.title: Joint-stock companies and the Amsterdam market
stops.blurb: The Dutch East India Company, or VOC, was founded in 1602 to trade with Asia. Its shares could be sold on to other investors, and a busy market in them and in related loans grew up in Amsterdam; by 1609 it was strong enough to set terms for government borrowing. With England's East India Company, the VOC is seen as an early model for the modern corporation.
stops.debate: Gelderblom and colleagues argue that features such as limited liability for managers were not planned at the start, but added step by step to solve the VOC's money problems.

stops.title: The Enlightenment begins
stops.blurb: Inspired by the success of the new science, writers in Europe and the Americas argued that human reason, rather than tradition or inherited authority, should guide both knowledge and public life. This movement, the Enlightenment, had centres in France, Scotland and the German lands. In 1784 the philosopher Immanuel Kant defined enlightenment as humanity's release from its self-incurred immaturity.
stops.dateNote: There is no agreed start date. Its roots lie in the scientific revolution, and the 1790s are a common end point.

p: For thousands of years after the ice age, the peoples of the Americas and those of Africa, Asia and Europe grew different crops and lived with different diseases. Ocean voyages after 1492 ended that separation within a few generations. Historians call the result the Columbian Exchange: the transfer of crops, diseases, ideas, technologies and people between the two halves of the world.

From the Americas came four staple crops: maize, potatoes, sweet potatoes and cassava (also called manioc). They gave more calories, or grew in places where older staples did poorly. Tomatoes, chili peppers, cacao, peanuts and pineapples added little in calories but changed cooking across the world, from paprika in Hungary to curries in India and chili in Korea and Thailand. Tobacco went the same way. In the other direction went wheat, rice, sugar cane, coffee, soybeans, oranges and bananas. Diseases travelled too, with terrible effect in the Americas.

Much of the evidence is the world's diet today. Nathan Nunn and Nancy Qian point out that the top consumers of potatoes and of cassava are now all countries outside the Americas, and that maize supplies a large share of daily calories in many of them. Written records track when crops arrived: Flynn and Giráldez note that American crops reached Chinese farms through the Manila galleons, the Spanish ships that crossed the Pacific each year from 1565.

To measure effects, economists compare places that could grow a new crop with places that could not, before and after it arrived. Using this method, Nunn and Qian estimate that the potato explains about 12 percent of the rise in population, and nearly half the rise in the share of people living in cities, in the Old World countries suited to it.

The size of the crop effects depends on the method and the period chosen, so figures like these are estimates, not settled facts. The origin of venereal syphilis, which spread across Europe in the 1490s, was argued over for centuries. Nunn and Qian review genetic work by Harper and colleagues that places the bacterium's closest relatives in South America, which supports an American origin, though accounts of similar symptoms and skeletons with similar-looking scars from before 1492 kept the question open for a long time.

Few people today eat a meal that the Columbian Exchange did not shape. New crops helped feed growing populations in China, Africa and Europe. At the same time, the exchange carried the diseases that emptied much of the Americas, and the plantation crops whose demand for labour drove the transatlantic slave trade. The same voyages that enriched diets on one side of the world brought catastrophe to the other.

The peoples of the Americas had been separated from Africa, Asia and Europe since the end of the ice age. They had never been exposed to smallpox, measles, whooping cough, chicken pox, typhus or malaria. When these diseases arrived after 1492, they spread through populations with no immunity. Outbreaks came again and again over the following century and more, alongside conquest and war. During the siege of Tenochtitlan in 1521, defenders died of disease and hunger as well as in battle.

The Taíno of Hispaniola, among the first peoples to meet Columbus's crews, had almost disappeared within fifty years. Central Mexico, with just under 15 million people in 1519, had about 1.5 million a century later. The historian Noble David Cook estimated that the least affected regions lost 80 percent of their people, the worst affected lost everyone, and a typical society lost 90 percent.
Written records begin only after contact. Disease often travelled ahead of the Europeans who wrote things down, so the earliest losses went unrecorded and first-hand counts may be too low.

Ancient DNA now helps identify the killers. In 2018, Åshild Vågene and colleagues studied a cemetery at Teposcolula-Yucundaa in Oaxaca, linked to an epidemic of 1545 to 1550 that people in Mexico called *cocoliztli*. They recovered genomes of *Salmonella enterica* Paratyphi C, a cause of enteric fever, from ten of the dead, making it a strong candidate for that outbreak.

The scale also shows up in the natural world. In 2019, Alexander Koch and colleagues combined 119 published population estimates with evidence of land use. They estimate about 60.5 million people lived in the Americas in 1492 and that about 90 percent died within a century, roughly 56 million people. As fields were abandoned, forest and grassland grew back on about 56 million hectares and took up carbon from the air.

How many people lived in the Americas in 1492 is one of the longest arguments in the field. Estimates have ranged from about 8 million (Kroeber, 1939) to over 110 million (Dobyns, 1966), and Nunn and Qian note that decades of research have not narrowed the range. Koch and colleagues give a likely range of about 45 to 78 million. Because early observers may have seen populations already thinned by disease, both high and low estimates have kept their defenders.

Nunn and Qian describe the devastation as far greater than that of the Black Death in Europe. The loss of so many workers, together with demand for plantation crops, helped drive the transatlantic slave trade. Koch and colleagues argue that the regrowth of forests on abandoned land helps explain half or more of a drop in carbon dioxide in the late 1500s and early 1600s, a sign that human history and the Earth's climate were already tied together.

From the early 1500s to 1866, ships based in Europe and the Americas carried captives from the coast of Africa across the Atlantic to be sold as slaves. SlaveVoyages, the main database of the trade, estimates that about 12.5 million people were forced aboard and about 10.7 million survived to land, almost all of them in the Americas.

The trade began slowly. About 2.2 million people were carried before 1700 and about 2.6 million more between 1700 and 1750. It then grew larger still, and nearly 2 million were carried in each 25-year period from 1751 to 1825.

West-Central Africa was the largest region of departure through most of the trade. Others included Senegambia, the Gold Coast, and the Bights of Benin and Biafra. About 95 percent of those who arrived in the Americas were landed in the Caribbean and South America, and less than 4 percent in North America. About 80 percent were taken to regions that grew sugar. Ships from seven ports, Rio de Janeiro, Bahia, Liverpool, London, Nantes, Bristol and Pernambuco, carried almost three-quarters of all the captives taken from Africa by sea.

Slaving voyages left records in archives on both sides of the Atlantic. The SlaveVoyages database gathers records of about 36,000 voyages across the Atlantic, some record of almost 80 percent of the ships that landed captives. From these, David Eltis and colleagues estimate the voyages that left no trace. On the voyages where deaths were recorded, about 12 percent of the people on board died during the crossing, called the Middle Passage. The rate varied from about 9 to nearly 20 percent depending on where the ship had left from.

The SlaveVoyages figures are widely used, but Eltis notes that other estimates of the trade's size exist, and the database is revised as new records come to light. Historians also debate the long-term effects on Africa. Using records of where captives came from, the economist Nathan Nunn found that the African countries from which the most people were taken are poorer today. He tested whether places that were already poorer were simply more exposed to the trade, and concluded that the slave trades held back economic development. Others caution that this kind of link is hard to prove, since places already in turmoil may both have lost more people and grown more slowly.

About 4.7 million people were taken before 1750, within the period of this chapter, and about 7.8 million after it. Most were taken to regions growing sugar for distant markets, and the plantation economies of the Americas depended on the labour of enslaved Africans and their descendants. The trade bound Africa, Europe and the Americas into one Atlantic system.

In 1545, rich silver ore was found in the Cerro Rico, the "rich hill" above Potosí in the Andes, in what is now Bolivia. The historian Kris Lane notes that the find is traditionally credited to an Andean prospector, Diego Huallpa. Under the viceroy Francisco de Toledo, Spanish rulers formalised and greatly expanded an older Andean labour draft, the mita. From 1573 to 1812 it forced Indigenous communities in Peru and Bolivia to send men to work in the mines. Large mills that used mercury to separate silver from crushed ore were built after 1572. In 1592, the year production peaked, Potosí held nearly 100,000 people.

The silver did not stay in Spain. Much of it went to China. In 1571 the Spanish founded Manila in the Philippines, and from then on galleons sailing between Acapulco and Manila carried American silver west and Chinese goods east. Japan also exported large amounts of silver to China until the late 1600s.

Historians reconstruct silver output and shipments from surviving colonial and trade records. Dennis Flynn and Arturo Giráldez brought these estimates together to follow silver around the world. They estimate that about 50 tons a year reached China across the Pacific after 1571, while tens of thousands of tons passed through Europe, by sea and overland, on their way to Asia.

Flynn and Giráldez argue that the key cause was in China. When the Ming state moved its money and taxes onto silver, the value of silver there roughly doubled compared with the rest of the world by the early 1500s. Mines in the Americas and Japan expanded to meet that demand. They argue against treating the societies of this period as separate or only weakly connected, and against writing their economic, environmental and population histories apart from one another. How far silver alone drove these connections remains a matter of interpretation.

The mita's effects are still measured today. Melissa Dell compared districts just inside and just outside the old mita boundary in Peru. She found that households inside it consume about a quarter less today, and their children are more often stunted.

Silver from Potosí and other mines tied the economies of the Americas, Europe and Asia together. It paid for Chinese goods in Europe and the Americas, and Flynn and Giráldez argue that the trade it financed carried American crops into China, helping its population more than double in the 1700s. Much of that silver was mined by Indigenous men under compulsion, through the mita, for more than two centuries.
